newsitem.title: USA: Gene may be linked to schizophrenia.
newsitem.headline: Gene may be linked to schizophrenia.

text.p: Scientists reported on Monday they have identified a gene that appears to be linked to schizophrenia and may also explain why schizophrenics tend to be heavy smokers.

Lead researcher Dr. Robert Freedman of Denver's VA Medical Center and the University of Colorado School of Medicine told Reuters the gene appeared to increase greatly the risk of developing the severe mental disorder, but not everyone with the gene becomes schizophrenic.
It is not yet known what other biological, experiential or environmental factors may interact with the gene to trigger the disease, which affects about 1.5 in 100 people, or four million Americans.

Schizophrenics can exhibit bizarre behavior including delusions and hearing voices. The disease usually appears in early adulthood and may have something to do with separation from home and family, one reason the Veterans Administration is interested since joining the military may be the first time a young man or women leaves home.
Freedman's findings, based on studies of nine extended families in which schizophrenia is common, appear in Tuesday's Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Because the families were from different racial and ethnic backgrounds, he believes the gene on chromosome 15 probably contributes to a large share of severe schizophrenia cases, not just cases in one segment of the population. There were 96 people in these families, 36 of whom were schizophrenic.

The gene is linked to a nicotinic receptor on chromosome 15, which may explain why so many schizophrenics are very heavy smokers. "Left to their own devices, many will smoke three or four packs a day, they'll smoke until it makes them nauseous," Freedman said. "Now we realize that they were trying to self-medicate."

Nicotine itself, however, is not a good therapy for schizophrenia, he said. Nicotinic receptors serve as brain "gatekeepers," helping decide which information is important and which background noise should be screened out. When the gatekeepers malfunction, information floods in and the brain is overloaded. That is part of what happens in schizophrenia.

Some of the people in the families Freedman studied had trouble screening out background noise such as a rattling air conditioner but did not develop schizophrenia. "We found that other people within the family of a schizophrenic person have inherited the filtering abnormality but are very normal."

Freedman hopes the finding will lead to improved treatment for schizophrenia. "We're spending a great deal of effort trying to figure out what the actual mutation is," he said. "We want to figure out what activates this particular gene and to develop new ways of attacking this genetic deficit."
